Medicaid’s real problem isn’t funding—it’s decades of bureaucratic bloat and mismanagement. Rural hospitals are collapsing because D.C. funnels cash into administrative overhead and red tape instead of frontline care. Take the $14B North Carolina gets annually: How much actually reaches patients? Audits show rampant fraud in state Medicaid programs, with billions lost to duplicate payments, ineligible enrollees, and inflated contracts.

The solution isn’t throwing more money at a broken system—it’s cutting the waste. Streamline eligibility, slash redundant middlemen, and redirect every dollar to rural clinics, not D.C. paper-pushers.

If hospitals close, blame the bureaucrats who turned Medicaid into a slush fund, not those demanding accountability.

The real crisis isn’t the bill—it’s decades of Medicaid abuse. Rural hospitals collapsed under bureaucratic bloat and unchecked non-citizen strain, not fiscal discipline. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act redirects $50 billion to rural healthcare while slashing waste that subsidized fraud.

North Carolina’s expansion added 673k to Medicaid rolls—how many paid into the system? Real reform prioritizes citizens who fund it, not globalist handouts.

The bill’s $10B/year rural hospital fund proves America First means fixing systemic rot, not preserving failure.

The PBM Reform Act is a critical step toward dismantling the opaque pricing schemes that have allowed pharmacy benefit managers to exploit patients and pharmacies for decades. With PBMs controlling 80% of the prescription drug market, their vertical integration and lack of transparency have directly fueled inflated drug costs—evidenced by $400M in Purdue Pharma rebates retained by PBMs instead of passing savings to consumers (Barron's 2024).

H.R. 950's mandate for PBM reporting on drug pricing benchmarks, rebate retention, and formulary manipulations aligns with exposing these middlemen's profit-driven tactics. The bill's ban on spread pricing in Medicaid and Medicare Part D transparency requirements will force PBMs to operate in daylight, ensuring pharmacies receive fair reimbursements rather than being strangled by below-cost payments.

This reform mirrors the accountability measures needed to break monopolistic control, as seen in the bipartisan push to delink PBM compensation from drug prices.
